cube.min_time()/max_time() reduce the temporal dimension per pixel/band using a min/max reducer on values, not on dates — each output pixel can come from a different timestamp, and different bands can effectively mix different acquisition dates. That's why the 'min' composite can look greener than 'max': it's not tied to any single date.

To get actual timestamps without downloading rasters: 1) Use the openEO process dimension_labels(cube, dimension='t') — in the Python client, cube.dimension_labels('t') — which returns just the temporal axis labels, not pixel data (still a tiny backend request, but no raster download). 2) Better, bypass the DataCube entirely and query the backend's STAC catalog directly with pystac-client (e.g. against the Copernicus Data Space STAC endpoint) using your bbox/collection/date filter — this returns exact item datetimes, is metadata-only, and is much cheaper than any openEO job. cube.metadata.extent only reflects the collection's declared bounds, not what's actually available for your filtered area, so it will never give you real per-scene dates.

This is almost always an interpreter mismatch: pip install customtkinter installed the package into a different Python environment than the one PyCharm/your script is actually running. Your traceback shows the script executing from inside a virtual environment folder — check that: 1) that venv is activated in the terminal where you ran pip (prompt should show (venv)), 2) PyCharm's project interpreter (File > Settings > Project > Python Interpreter) is set to that same venv's python.exe, not the system Python or a different venv. Run pip list from inside the exact interpreter PyCharm uses to confirm they match. Safest fix: with the venv activated, run python -m pip install customtkinter (using python -m pip rather than a possibly-different pip on PATH), then restart PyCharm/the run configuration. If you have multiple Python installs, where python and where pip on Windows will often show they resolve to different locations, which is the classic cause of pip list showing a package while import still fails in the IDE.

Color(0) is the documented, safe idiom for the empty flag — it's explicitly used in the stdlib docs and works fine under STRICT boundary since 0 trivially satisfies any boundary rule.

For 'full', prefer ~Color(0) over Color(-1). Flag's __invert__ (since the 3.11 Flag rewrite) is defined in terms of the class's own known members — it computes the complement within the defined bits, i.e. invert(empty) == all-members-set — rather than relying on raw two's-complement integer semantics. Color(-1) happens to work today because of how STRICT boundary canonicalizes negative values against the mask of defined bits, but that's an implementation detail of value coercion, not a documented contract, so it's more exposed to change across versions. ~Color(0) only uses operations (invert applied to a canonical empty member) that are explicitly part of Flag's public behavior. functools.reduce(operator.or_, Color) also works for 'full' and is fully explicit, but is more verbose with no real benefit over ~Color(0).

Full NTFS access in the Properties > Security tab doesn't rule out the other common causes of WinError 13 on Windows:

1) Another process has the file open/locked — most likely candidate given the folder structure (looks like a game's data files): the game/editor that owns these .blk files, or an antivirus real-time scan, can hold a lock that only shows up as permission denied from Python's side.
2) The file's own Read-only attribute (not the folder's) — right-click the specific .blk file > Properties > General tab > uncheck Read-only (separate from the Security/ACL tab you already checked).
3) If First_folder/Second_folder is inside OneDrive/Dropbox/Google Drive, background sync can transiently lock a file right as you try to write it.
4) Try running Spyder as Administrator once, to isolate whether it's a privilege issue vs a lock issue.

Also wrap the write in a short retry/backoff, since transient AV/sync locks often clear within a second.

The question body got cut off before the actual problem/error is shown, so this is necessarily general guidance: for sites like Sofascore that guard their API behind JS-set cookies/tokens, warming up in a real browser context then calling the API is the right pattern, but call the API through Playwright's own request context — await context.request.get(url) — rather than a separate requests/httpx call, since APIRequestContext automatically reuses the cookies and headers the browser page just collected. Also set a realistic User-Agent and Referer header, wait for the homepage to actually settle (wait_until='networkidle' or wait for a specific selector) before hitting the API, and expect some responses may still be blocked by bot-detection (Cloudflare/DataDome) that Playwright alone can't fully bypass — you may need playwright-stealth or similar. Note Sofascore's terms of service generally prohibit scraping their API directly, worth checking before building on this. Sharing the actual error/traceback would allow a more targeted answer.

Two likely causes. First, shape/ordering: xgboost's custom multiclass objective expects grad and hess flattened in row-major (sample-major) order matching how it internally stores multi-class predictions — if you return a 2D (n_samples, num_classes) array where xgboost expects a flattened 1D array (or vice-versa depending on your xgboost version/API — native Booster vs sklearn, and whether multi_strategy='multi_output_tree' is set), the optimizer silently trains on garbage and looks like it doesn't train at all. Always flatten grad/hess consistently with how predt is shaped when it's passed in.

Second, and more likely given a hand-derived focal-loss Hessian: xgboost requires hess >= 0 per row for tree building to make sense, and it clips/handles non-positive Hessians in ways that can stall learning; a sign error in a manually-derived multiclass focal-loss Hessian (very easy to get wrong) commonly produces negative values. Validate grad/hess against autograd (torch.autograd) or finite differences before trusting the closed-form derivative, and print min/max of hess each round to check positivity.

Most likely cause: sqlite3's adapter registry keys on the exact type via type(obj), not via isinstance — so register_adapter(date, date_adapter) only fires when you insert an object whose exact type is datetime.date. Since datetime.datetime is a subclass of date, inserting a datetime instance (e.g. from datetime.now()) instead of a plain date won't match your registered adapter, and sqlite3 silently falls back to its deprecated built-in converter, triggering the warning. Check exactly what type you're passing into the INSERT — if it's ever a datetime rather than a date, you need a second explicit registration: sqlite3.register_adapter(datetime, datetime_adapter). Also double check you registered the adapter before opening/using the connection that performs the INSERT (registration is global but must happen before first use), and that you're not accidentally going through a second sqlite3.connect() call somewhere else that runs before your adapter registration executes. If both types are covered and it still warns, print type() of the value right before the INSERT to confirm what's actually being adapted.

query()'s 16384 cap is a hard per-request limit, so for ~3M rows you need to paginate rather than pull it all at once. The purpose-built tool for this is Milvus's QueryIterator (pymilvus): collection.query_iterator(batch_size=1000, expr='', output_fields=[...]), then repeatedly call .next() until it returns an empty list. It's designed exactly for full-collection export/scroll and works fine with a string primary key since it paginates internally using the PK as a cursor rather than requiring you to construct numeric ranges yourself.

For a full collection migration (not just export), consider milvus-backup (the official Milvus backup/restore tool) instead of query+insert — it exports a collection's data and schema and can restore/import it into a new collection, which is more robust and much faster than manually iterating 3M records and re-inserting them, and avoids hand-rolling pagination, retries, and dynamic-field schema mapping yourself.

getmany() with a timeout just returns an empty dict when nothing arrives in that window — it does not raise when the broker itself is down. aiokafka's underlying client handles broker disconnects by retrying/reconnecting internally and logs that via its own logger (logging.getLogger('aiokafka')) rather than propagating an exception up through getmany(), which is why you only ever see 'Try consume' with no error hitting your except block — by design, transient broker outages are meant to be transparent/self-healing, not raised to caller code.

To actually detect/log a down broker: 1) configure logging so aiokafka's internal WARNING/ERROR logs (connection failures, metadata refresh failures) are visible in your app's output — that's the real signal Kafka is unreachable. 2) Add an explicit health check, e.g. periodically inspect consumer._client.ready(...) or the coordinator's connection state, or wrap consumer.start()/commit() (which can raise KafkaConnectionError/RequestTimedOutError) rather than expecting getmany() itself to surface the failure.

find_tables()/table detection is the wrong primitive here — it looks for grid-like ruling lines or aligned text, which newspaper columns don't reliably have, so it will only ever catch layouts that coincidentally look tabular. For article segmentation you generally need two passes: (1) find column boundaries from large vertical whitespace gaps in page.extract_words() x-positions, (2) within each column, find article breaks from horizontal whitespace gaps between text blocks and/or headline detection using font size (extract_words(extra_attrs=['size','fontname']) — a jump to a larger/bolder font usually marks a new article's headline), then merge consecutive lines between headline breaks into one bounding box per article.

Hand-rolled gap/heuristic clustering with pdfplumber can work but is fragile on irregular newspaper grids. For something more robust, look at document layout analysis models purpose-built for this (LayoutParser with a PubLayNet-trained Detectron2/PaddleDetection model, or Docling), which segment multi-column print pages into article-level regions directly rather than relying on ruling lines.

Decimal isn't really a better tool for float-vs-float comparison — the imprecision in an already-computed float comes from its binary representation, and Decimal can't retroactively fix that, so for testing numerical/scientific code your existing pytest.approx()/math.isclose()-with-epsilon approach is the right one and Decimal wouldn't help there.

Decimal's real use case is when the arithmetic itself must be done in exact base-10, not just compared afterward — money, invoicing, tax, accounting, anything with legally/contractually defined rounding rules. There you want 0.1 + 0.2 to equal exactly 0.30 and sums of currency amounts to never accumulate binary rounding drift in the first place, with explicit control over precision and rounding mode via decimal.getcontext(). So the dividing line isn't comparison strategy, it's domain: use Decimal when the underlying quantities are inherently decimal/discrete (currency, quantities with defined decimal places) and correctness of the arithmetic itself matters; use float plus tolerance comparison for continuous numerical/scientific computation where binary floating point is the natural representation.

Generalize get_concat_v to take a list, then chunk the folder's files into groups of 4:

import os
from PIL import Image

def concat_v(images):
    w = max(im.width for im in images)
    h = sum(im.height for im in images)
    dst = Image.new('RGB', (w, h), 'white')
    y = 0
    for im in images:
        dst.paste(im, (0, y))
        y += im.height
    return dst

folder, out = 'images', 'output'
os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)
files = sorted(f for f in os.listdir(folder) if f.lower().endswith(('.png', '.jpg', '.jpeg')))

for i in range(0, len(files), 4):
    chunk = files[i:i+4]
    imgs = [Image.open(os.path.join(folder, f)) for f in chunk]
    concat_v(imgs).save(os.path.join(out, f'concat_{i//4+1}.png'))

For 9 images this naturally yields 3 outputs (4, 4, then 1 leftover) since the last slice just has fewer items — concat_v works fine with a single image too. Sort filenames first so grouping is deterministic.

The mangled name (a tilde-prefixed leftover folder such as ~atplotlib) is a classic remnant of a previously interrupted pip uninstall/upgrade sitting in site-packages; removing it was correct. Requirement already satisfied now confirms matplotlib 3.10.7 is installed into your Anaconda base environment's site-packages — but if the Jupyter kernel you're actually running isn't that same Anaconda base interpreter (a different conda env, or a stale kernelspec pointing elsewhere), import will still fail there.

Confirm by running, inside the notebook itself: import sys; print(sys.executable) — and compare that to your Anaconda installation's python.exe path. If they differ, either switch the notebook's kernel (Kernel > Change Kernel) to the matching environment, or install matplotlib into that exact interpreter's env. Also fully restart the kernel (not just rerun cells) after any install, since a previously failed import can be cached in the running kernel process. Going forward, prefer conda install -c conda-forge matplotlib over pip inside an Anaconda env to avoid pip/conda package-state conflicts like this one.

No single built-in covers all reductions, but the standard idioms:

Mean (what you have) is the canonical approach: (x*mask).sum(dim)/mask.sum(dim).

Max/min: fill masked-out entries with the reduction's identity element first, then use the ordinary reduction:
x.masked_fill(~mask, float('-inf')).max(dim=1)
x.masked_fill(~mask, float('inf')).min(dim=1)

PyTorch also has a prototype torch.masked (MaskedTensor) API meant to be the proper built-in answer:
mt = torch.masked.masked_tensor(x.float(), mask)
mt.mean(dim=1), mt.amax(dim=1), mt.amin(dim=1), mt.sum(dim=1)
This handles mean/amax/amin/sum consistently without manual identity-element juggling, but as of recent PyTorch releases it's still labeled prototype/beta, so API details can change between versions — fine for research code, worth pinning your torch version if you depend on it in production.

Use a stable descending argsort so ties keep their original (first-occurrence) index order, then take the first n:

def generalized_argmax(x, n):
    order = torch.argsort(x, descending=True, stable=True)
    return torch.sort(order[:n]).values

argsort's stable=True (PyTorch >= 1.9) guarantees equal values keep their relative input order rather than an arbitrary one, which is exactly what 'first n maximum values, including duplicates in order' needs. For x = [2,1,4,1,4,2,1,1], stable descending order is [2,4,0,5,1,3,6,7] (the two 4's by index, then the two 2's by index, then the 1's); taking the first 4 gives {2,4,0,5}, and sorting ascending gives [0,2,4,5] — matching your expected output.

torch.topk(x, n) returns n largest values/indices too, but its tie-breaking order isn't documented/guaranteed the way stable=True is, so prefer argsort(stable=True) if you need deterministic first-occurrence tie-breaking.

A few standard options depending on whether you want viewable vs actually runnable:

Viewable only, zero setup: push it to a public GitHub repo — GitHub renders .ipynb files automatically in the browser. Or paste any URL to the notebook into nbviewer.org for a clean rendered view.

Actually runnable in-browser, no local install:
1) Google Colab — upload the notebook or open it from GitHub/Drive, then share the Colab link (set sharing to 'Anyone with the link'); viewers can run all cells for free.
2) Binder (mybinder.org) — point it at a public GitHub repo containing the notebook plus a requirements.txt/environment.yml; it builds a temporary live Jupyter environment and gives you a shareable link where anyone can execute cells with no install, good for reproducible environments.
3) Kaggle Notebooks or Deepnote are similar hosted/runnable alternatives.

Best combo for public sharing: a GitHub repo (viewing + version control) plus a Binder badge in the README (one-click execution).

This is really two systems combined, not one:

1) The Q&A-over-company-data part is a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pipeline: chunk and embed your internal documents into a vector database (Chroma, FAISS, pgvector, Pinecone), retrieve the most relevant chunks per user query, and pass them as context to an LLM to generate the answer. Use a framework like LangChain or LlamaIndex to wire this together. Private typically means either self-hosting an open model (Llama/Mistral via Ollama/vLLM) or using an enterprise API plan with no data retention/training on your data.

2) Stock levels and reorder suggestions are not something an LLM should compute from scratch — write that as ordinary business logic/SQL against your inventory database (e.g. reorder_qty = forecasted_demand_over_lead_time + safety_stock - current_stock), expose it as a function/tool, and let the chatbot call that tool via function-calling/agentic tool-use rather than asking the LLM to reason numbers directly.

Those two error messages together suggest a routing/permissioning conflict rather than a simple field typo: PostToATS is only meaningful for orders routed to specific ATS destinations, and it looks like your account/order combination is being rejected both for including it and (per the second message) for the order type requiring it, depending on how IB's backend resolves routing for PEG BEST plus IBKRATS.

Try removing o.postToAts entirely (don't set it at all, rather than 0 or 1) and let IBKRATS routing handle ATS participation implicitly — PEG BEST orders are generally only valid on IBKRATS to begin with, so the explicit flag may be redundant/conflicting. If that still fails, this is likely account-permissioning (PostToATS access needs to be explicitly enabled by IB for your account) or a TWS/API-version-specific quirk rather than something fixable purely in your Order object — worth filing directly with IB API support, since this is too IB-internals-specific to fully resolve from client code alone.
